content.title: About
content.content: Beef Wellington is a classic British dish consisting of a beef tenderloin coated with a mushroom duxelles and a layer of ham or prosciutto, wrapped in puff pastry and baked until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is named after the Duke of Wellington, who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
It is traditionally served at festive occasions, especially Christmas and New Year’s dinners.
There are many variations: some recipes use veal, turkey, or even plant‑based substitutes instead of beef.
The pastry must stay cold; otherwise it won’t puff and will lose its flaky texture.
Mushroom duxelles are often enriched with shallots, thyme, and a splash of brandy for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef tenderloin provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron and zinc, supporting immune function and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef Wellington supplies B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial mushrooms
items.content: The mushroom duxelles add antioxidants, fiber, and vitamin D, which are good for bone health.

items.title: Balanced fats
items.content: Puff pastry and ham contribute monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The pastry and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: A significant amount of saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergens
items.content: Puff pastry typically contains wheat flour and sometimes dairy, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure the interior reaches at least 63 °C (145 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Beef Wellington hot, sliced into portions. It is commonly accompanied by a sauce (such as red‑wine reduction or mushroom sauce), roasted vegetables, and mashed potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked Beef Wellington can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, tightly wrapped. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight container for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven to restore the crisp pastry before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft NFS breadsticks are tender, lightly toasted sticks made from wheat flour following a classic recipe. They have a soft texture, a subtle buttery aroma, and a mildly sweet flavor, making them perfect for snacking or as a side to meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Breadsticks originated in Italy as “grissini,” but the soft version became popular in the United States in the 1970s.
NFS (Not For Sale) is an internal company code indicating the product is intended for internal café use only.
Soft sticks are often served with dips such as marinara, cheese sauce, or hummus.
Unlike crunchy sticks, soft ones retain moisture longer, allowing them to be used in hot dishes like casseroles.
Traditionally they are made without preservatives, relying on fresh ingredients.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Breadsticks provide a quick source of energy thanks to the carbohydrates they contain.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The wheat flour used supplies B1, B2, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Soft sticks usually contain little fat, especially when prepared without added butter.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture makes them gentle on the stomach, suitable for children and seniors.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used, the fiber content increases, aiding digestion.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The product contains gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of the simple carbs, breadsticks can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions are heavily salted; those monitoring sodium should choose unsalted options.

items.title: Short shelf life
items.content: The soft texture makes the product more prone to spoilage; store in a dry cool place and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breadsticks can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, dipped in sauces, added to salads, used as a base for canapés, or served alongside soups and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, refrigerate; they will stay soft for up to a week.

cabbage-green-cooked-with-butter-or-marg.title: Cabbage, green, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Green cabbage is a leafy cruciferous vegetable. When cooked with butter or margarine it becomes tender and aromatic while retaining most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One cup of cooked cabbage provides over 100 % of the daily recommended vitamin C.
Cabbage contains glucosinolates that support detoxification and have anti‑cancer properties.
Fresh cabbage can be kept in the fridge for up to two weeks and frozen for up to a year.
Traditional Russian cuisine often sautés cabbage in butter, enhancing the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Cabbage leaves are used as natural wrappers for fermenting sauerkraut.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, collagen synthesis, and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Provides antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Cabbage is high in potassium and low in sodium, helping to regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cabbage contains raffinose, which can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with anticoagulants
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin K may reduce the effectiveness of blood‑thinning medications.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to cabbage.

items.title: Oxalic acid content
items.content: Excessive intake of oxalic acid can contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the cabbage in butter or margarine for 5‑10 minutes, seasoning with salt and spices. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or incorporate into stews and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh green cabbage in the refrigerator in a perforated bag for up to 10 days. Store cooked cabbage in an airtight container in the fridge for 3‑4 days.

cheese-sandwich-cheddar-cheese-on-wheat-.title: Cheddar Cheese Sandwich on Wheat Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A cheddar cheese sandwich on wheat bread is a classic light snack consisting of slices of mature cheddar cheese placed between two pieces of whole‑grain wheat bread. The combination of aromatic, slightly sharp cheese and a soft, lightly crisp crust makes it popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheddar cheese originates from the English county of Somerset, where it has been produced for over 800 years.
Wheat bread used in the sandwich is rich in fiber and B‑vitamins.
Sandwiches became mass‑popular in the United States in the early 20th century due to their convenience.
Cheddar can be aged from a few months to several years, developing flavors from mild to very sharp.
Traditional English cheddar sandwiches are often served with mustard or pickles.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheddar provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheddar is high in calcium for bone health and contains small amounts of vitamin D that aid calcium absorption.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread supplies dietary fiber, improving digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread offers thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Some aged cheddars contain live cultures that can support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheddar contains lactose; those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheddar can be salty, so individuals monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to dairy products.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense (about 350 kcal), so it should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be served warm, lightly toasted until the bread is golden, or cold. It pairs well with lettuce, tomato, mustard, or a light spread of mayo.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep cheese wrapped separately and bread in a dry place to prevent sogginess.

coffee-creamer-liquid-fat-free-flavored.title: Coffee Creamer, Liquid, Fat Free, Flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee creamer is a liquid additive for coffee that contains no fat and is enriched with flavorings. It dissolves quickly, giving the drink a creamy texture and a variety of taste notes without adding caloric fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat‑free creamer often uses plant‑based protein hydrolysates as fat substitutes.
Flavored versions may include vanilla, caramel, nut, or spice profiles.
The liquid form allows easy dosing in automatic coffee machines.
Some brands add probiotics or vitamins for extra health benefits.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: The absence of fat makes the creamer suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Enhances flavor without sugar
items.content: Flavorings provide sweet or aromatic taste without added sugar.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: Liquid consistency blends instantly with hot or cold coffee.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Some variants are fortified with probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B2 and B12 are often added to support energy metabolism.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Formulations may contain soy or dairy proteins that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: Some consumers prefer to avoid synthetic flavors and sweeteners.

items.title: Sugar content in flavored versions
items.content: Certain flavors may contain small amounts of sugar, which should be considered by people with diabetes.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Improper storage after opening can lead to rapid spoilage.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 10–20 ml of creamer to a prepared cup of coffee and stir. It can also be used in cold drinks, lattes, cappuccinos, and dessert sauces. For automatic machines, dispense the creamer from a dedicated reservoir.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 2–6 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, use within 7–10 days. Do not allow the product to freeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Jam is a sweet spread made by cooking fruit or berries with sugar until it reaches a thick consistency. It retains the aroma and some vitamins of the original fruit while providing a convenient way to preserve fruit for long periods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial jam appeared in the 19th century in the United States.
There are more than 200 varieties of jam, ranging from classic strawberry to exotic mango‑chili blends.
Traditionally, jams are canned in glass jars that, after sterilization, can be stored for years.
Sugar in jam not only sweetens but also acts as a preservative, slowing microbial growth.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Fruit jam retains some vitamin C, which supports the immune system and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols from berries and fruits remain in jam, helping to combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of dietary fiber in jam can aid regular bowel movements.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar may contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: People allergic to certain fruits (e.g., strawberries) may experience reactions when consuming jam.

items.title: Preservatives in industrial products
items.content: Some commercial jams contain additives (pectin, preservatives) that may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jam is perfect for spreading on bread, toast, pancakes, and also as a filling for pastries, yogurts, and desserts. It can be added to sauces or used in marinades for meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store opened jam in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed jar for 4–6 weeks. Unopened jars should be kept in a cool, dry place away from direct light.

content.title: About
content.content: Papad (also spelled papadum) are thin, crisp wafers made from rice or lentil flour, traditionally used in Indian cuisine. They are prepared by dry‑frying in a pan or baking in an oven until golden and crunchy. Papad has a light, slightly nutty flavor and a delicate texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Papad is often served as an appetizer or side dish with curries and other Indian meals.
Traditionally it is made from lentil, chickpea or rice flour, sometimes seasoned with cumin, black pepper or other spices.
In India papad is considered a “food of the gods” and is commonly offered during religious festivals.
There are many regional varieties, ranging from ultra‑thin translucent sheets to thicker, more robust versions.
Papad can be stored in a dry place for several months and, once opened, should be kept in an airtight container.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Papad is cooked without added oil, making it a low‑calorie snack.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: The legume‑based flour provides dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Legume flours contribute a modest amount of plant‑based protein, useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains micronutrients
items.content: Depending on the ingredients, papad may supply iron, magnesium and zinc.

items.title: Gluten‑free option
items.content: Rice‑flour papad offers a gluten‑free alternative for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some papad varieties are salted; people monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: If made from lentil or chickpea flour, papad can trigger reactions in individuals allergic to legumes.

items.title: Digestive discomfort in large amounts
items.content: High fiber content may cause bloating or gas if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Papad is served as a crunchy snack, often accompanied by chutney, raita or dips. It can be broken into pieces and added to salads, soups, or used as a base for canapés. For extra crispness, briefly fry it in a dry pan before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep papad in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Properly stored, it remains crisp for several months.

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ. In this version it is served with fresh tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce, without added fat, making it a light and nutritious dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains more fiber and nutrients compared with white rice.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
The dish contains no added fats, so its calorie count comes only from the rice and tomatoes.
Tomatoes provide vitamin C, potassium, and folate.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to stabilize blood sugar.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nervous system health, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene has strong antioxidant properties and may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps control blood sugar levels, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of some minerals when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose organically certified rice to minimize exposure to residual pesticides.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the rice until tender, then stir in fresh tomatoes, tomato sauce, or puree, and season with herbs such as basil or oregano. The dish can be served as a side or a light main course.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato sauce for vegetables is a ready‑made sauce made from ripe tomatoes, aromatic herbs and spices, designed to dress and cook a variety of vegetable dishes. It has a rich tomato flavor, mild sweetness and a hint of acidity, making it a versatile addition to salads, casseroles, stews and grilled vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes used in the sauce are often greenhouse‑grown to ensure a consistent taste year‑round.
Traditional Italian tomato sauce recipes include basil, oregano and garlic, giving it a characteristic aroma.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene – a powerful antioxidant that gives tomatoes their bright red color.
In some countries the sauce is served cold as a dip for fresh vegetable sticks.
Heat‑processed tomatoes in sauce become more digestible, and their nutrients more bioavailable.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties, supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and beta‑carotene
items.content: Support vision, skin health and immunity.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Tomato sauce is typically low in calories, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Helps regulate digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some ready‑made sauces can be high in salt; people with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Sugar is sometimes added to improve taste, which may be undesirable for blood‑glucose management.

items.title: Allergy to spices
items.content: The sauce may contain garlic, onion or herbs that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain commercial sauces contain preservatives; choose additive‑free options if preferred.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the sauce to dress salads, as a base for vegetable casseroles, stews, grilled vegetables, or as a dip for fresh veggie sticks. It can also be warmed in a pan with a splash of olive oil to deepen the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in the refrigerator after opening in a tightly sealed jar. Once opened, it typically lasts 5‑7 days. Avoid contaminating the sauce with dirty utensils to prevent spoilage.

turkey-drumstick-roasted-skin-not-eaten.title: Turkey, drumstick, roasted, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The drumstick is the leg portion containing meat and bone. Roasted without skin, turkey drumstick meat is tender, moderately dry in texture, and low in fat, making it a popular choice for healthy eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated over 2,000 years ago by Indigenous peoples of North America.
Turkey drumsticks provide more protein per gram than most other poultry cuts.
Roasting without skin preserves a higher amount of B‑vitamins, especially niacin and vitamin B6.
Turkey meat is a staple in traditional U.S. dishes such as Thanksgiving dinner.
Turkey contains more iron than chicken, beneficial for preventing anemia.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey drumstick delivers high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin reduces saturated fat content, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B3, B6, and B12 aid metabolism, nervous system function, and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Consuming turkey does not cause rapid spikes in blood glucose.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey proteins.

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: If the drumstick is pre‑marinated, watch the added salt content.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large portions can increase uric acid levels in people prone to gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted turkey drumstick without skin can be served hot as a main dish, sliced for salads, added to soups, or used in sandwiches. Garnish with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or a light yogurt‑based sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw drumsticks refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. After roasting, store cooled meat in an airtight container in the fridge for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of ≥ 74 °C before eating.
